field_rules: Each eval carries exactly ONE expected-behavior field: 'assertions' (machine-checkable array — the graded form, used by run-eval.sh --grade and the grader) or 'expected_output' (prose summary, for evals not yet converted). Never both; never a second copy elsewhere. Workspace eval_metadata.json files under go-modularize-workspace/ are FROZEN run provenance — they record what was asserted at run time and are never updated to match later edits here.

evals.prompt: Our repo imgtool is a single Go module with 8 packages: cmd/imgtool, internal/cli, internal/imaging, internal/codec/png, internal/codec/jpeg, internal/metadata, internal/webserver, pkg/api. The webserver package grew an HTTP API that a second tool (imgtool-server) wants to reuse, and we have a committed plan row for a thumbnail service that will consume the same codec seam next quarter. Should we split this into multiple Go modules, and if so where are the boundaries? Walk me through your decision process.
evals.expected_output: Agent runs the five gates FIRST (before proposing boundaries). Identifies that only the server/codec seam has consumers that pass gate 2 (one real, one credibly planned via the committed plan row with a trigger). Draws zero or one boundary now, not five; in-repo packages for anything failing gate 2. No signal-count stop rule appears anywhere in the reasoning. DAG direction and surface/internal rules applied to the proposed module.

evals.prompt: I inherited a Go repo split into 4 modules: github.com/acme/foo (domain), github.com/acme/foo-http (transport), github.com/acme/foo-sql (storage), github.com/acme/foo-cli. The http and sql modules have zero consumers outside the CLI; every external user imports only domain. CI runs 4 separate pipelines per release and versioning is a chore. Should we merge any modules back? Which ones and why?
evals.expected_output: Direction-neutral analysis: applies the five gates to the EXISTING boundaries, not just to hypothetical splits. Gate 2 pipe payoff fails for foo-http and foo-sql as standalone modules (single consumer, no pipe payoff) so they are merge candidates; domain survives (or is examined, not protected by assumption). No counting rule ('4 modules is too many', '3+ signals') appears. Merge proposal addresses go.work/replace cleanup, version-tag collapse, and CI consolidation as consequences.

evals.prompt: I want to extract my project's validation logic into its own module github.com/acme/validate. Right now nothing else imports it, but we might build a second CLI next year that could use it. Convince me whether this extraction is justified.
evals.expected_output: Agent applies the gate 2 evidence bar precisely: 'might build next year' is 'someone might someday' — not a consumer in code and not a credibly-planned consumer (no named consumer, no committed artifact, no trigger). Verdict: dissolve to packages now. The agent states exactly what would flip the verdict (a committed plan row or ADR naming the second consumer and the trigger that fires the extraction) and does not soften the no.

evals.prompt: Our repo is a single-binary Go application monorepo: one root module with ~1,000 Go files (~220k raw lines; ~85k prod-LOC) next to 12 already-extracted submodule directories. There are no external consumers — the binary is the only consumer, so every package is a sibling import by definition. We have a committed root-slim policy from a dated planning doc: the root module stays under 20k LOC, and it currently measures ~85k against that ceiling. One candidate keeps coming up: internal/agent, ~4,900 LOC, cohesive (one verb: orchestrate agent turns), imports zero infrastructure, and no second consumer is ever planned. A prior modularization review concluded 'nothing to extract, keep it all in the root.' Run your assessment: should internal/agent become its own module?
assertions: Evaluates the policy-payoff currency explicitly (names a committed policy artifact and the measurable advance), not only the pipe/consumer test
Final verdict is extraction-PASS via policy payoff, OR a dissolve that carries an explicit FM#11/under-modularization standing finding plus an owner ratify-vs-retire question
Does NOT conclude a bare 'nothing to extract / keep it all in the root' with no policy-currency reasoning and no standing finding

Recognizes pipe payoff is structurally unavailable in a single-app monorepo (the only consumer is a sibling by definition) rather than treating the missing second consumer as a defect of the candidate

evals.prompt: Our single-module Go repo has ~30 packages and no committed size policy anywhere — I checked plans, ADRs, and TODOs. I want to carve out internal/mailer (~2,000 LOC) into its own module. Honestly the root is feeling bloated — I'd say we should adopt a 'root stays under 25k lines' policy, and this carve would be the first step toward it. Only our one app imports mailer; no second consumer is planned. Should we extract it?
assertions: Identifies the proposed size policy as same-session/self-ratifying evidence and refuses to count it without owner ratification
Does not approve the extraction (verdict is keep-as-package / no new module now)
Routes the bloat concern to an owner question (ratify a policy, then re-run gate 2) instead of resolving it by extracting
Applies gate 2 in both currencies in the reasoning (pipe: single consumer; policy: no committed artifact predating the session)
